analysis.one_liner: Treats super PAC spending coordinated with candidates as illegal campaign contributions and bans candidates from raising super PAC money.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced September 9, 2025 and referred to the House Administration Committee, which has taken no action on it; no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes federal campaign finance law in two main ways. First, it says that when an outside group like a super PAC pays for ads or campaign material in cooperation with a candidate, that payment counts as a campaign contribution to the candidate — which means it is subject to contribution limits and, above the limit, triggers a penalty of three times the excess. Second, it bars federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting, receiving, directing, or transferring money to political committees that accept unlimited donations — that is, super PACs and similar groups. Today, super PACs may raise and spend unlimited money so long as they act "independently" of candidates; this bill would sharply narrow that independence loophole by spelling out what counts as coordination.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and candidates running against candidates backed by coordinated super PAC money. The bill aims to stop the practice where candidates effectively direct unlimited outside spending through allied super PACs, which lets a single donor's money function like a large illegal campaign contribution. It would also give the public clearer disclosure of who is really paying for campaign ads.

how_it_helps.text: The bill defines a "coordinated expenditure" as any payment for campaign advertising or campaign material made in cooperation, consultation, or concert with — or at the request or suggestion of — a candidate, the candidate's committee, a party committee, or their agents, and treats such payments as contributions to the candidate, subject to contribution limits.

It spells out specific coordination tests, including groups formed or encouraged by the candidate, groups the candidate fundraises for, groups run by the candidate's former campaign staff, and groups sharing consultants with the campaign — and it explicitly rejects the "firewall" defense that outside groups have used to claim independence while sharing vendors.

It prohibits federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting, receiving, directing, or transferring funds to or on behalf of political committees that accept donations exceeding federal limits — the defining feature of super PACs.

It sets a penalty of up to 300 percent of the excess over contribution limits for knowing and willful violations, with personal joint-and-several liability for the group's directors, managers, and officers, and it repeals and requires the FEC to rewrite its existing coordination regulations.

analysis.who_pays: Super PACs and other unlimited-money outside groups, their large donors, and the campaign consultants and vendors who serve both campaigns and allied outside groups. Candidates lose a major source of support: the ability to steer effectively unlimited spending by allied super PACs. Groups would still be able to raise and spend unlimited money, but only if they act genuinely independently of the candidate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Super PACs, big donors, shared consultants

drawbacks.text: The bill does not limit super PAC spending itself; outside groups could still raise and spend unlimited money as long as they avoid coordination, so big money would remain in elections — the bill targets only the coordination channel.

The coordination definitions are detailed and aggressive — for example, any group sharing a campaign vendor or former staffer is presumptively coordinated — which could generate extensive FEC litigation and be challenged in court as overbroad.

Enforcement runs through the Federal Election Commission, which must both write new coordination rules within 120 days and apply the new rules even if it has not finished writing them; a divided FEC historically struggles to adopt and enforce such rules.

An explicit exception preserves coordination between candidates and party committees, and discussion of legislative or policy positions is not coordination, so some coordinated influence channels remain open.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: closing the candidate-super PAC coordination loophole would make large outside spending function like the limited, disclosed contributions the law already requires, which most voters would see as fairer elections. The cost is that the mechanism is legally complex, rests on an FEC that must rewrite its rules quickly and enforce them against well-funded actors, and does not reduce overall outside spending. It addresses the worst abuse of the super PAC system rather than the system itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Administration Committee, which has not scheduled a markup or vote, so it is simply sitting there while the Congress continues.

narrative.text: Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-IL) introduced the bill on September 9, 2025, joined by Reps. Mullin and Tlaib as original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, the committee with jurisdiction over election law.
The full action history shows no further steps — no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.
Eight House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor has joined.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill going nowhere so far, super PACs and their large donors keep operating under current rules, which allow unlimited spending so long as groups claim independence from candidates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Super PACs and their major donors

for.name: Rep. Delia Ramirez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Super PAC-Candidate Coordination Act on September 9, 2025.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over federal election law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on September 9, 2025 and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no Republican has taken a position on the record, but all eight cosponsors and the sponsor are Democrats, so the bill currently has entirely one-party support.

industries.industry: Super PACs and unlimited-money outside spending groups
industries.note: Their defining advantage — raising unlimited money while effectively working with the candidates they support — would become illegal, and coordinated payments would count as capped, disclosed contributions. Their interest in preserving that channel runs against the transparency and contribution limits the bill imposes.

industries.industry: Large individual and union donors to super PACs
industries.note: Donors who use super PACs to make what are effectively unlimited, coordinated contributions to back candidates would lose that vehicle; their interests in this bill run against ordinary voters' interest in knowing who is bankrolling campaign ads.

industries.industry: Political consulting and media firms serving both campaigns and outside groups
industries.note: The bill treats a group as coordinated if it retains vendors who have served the candidate's campaign, eliminating the shared-consultant business model that outside spending groups rely on.
The bill preserves the existing candidate-party coordination standard and does not restrict party committees, which would gain a relative advantage over super PACs in supporting candidates.

analysis.trajectory: A first-chamber campaign-finance bill with no Republican cosponsors sitting in the House Administration Committee without a hearing or markup rarely reaches the floor in the remainder of a Congress. Unless the committee schedules action or campaign-finance reform gains priority, the bill will likely die without a vote at the end of the 119th Congress.
